question: Tell me about a time you kept the customer and the product in mind when others wanted to chase a technically interesting problem. How did you steer the conversation?

raiseTranscript.text: On my first project, the team wanted to add a custom caching layer with new algorithms because it sounded novel. I pulled up the support tickets showing customers mostly complained about login latency, not throughput.
I suggested we benchmark the existing Redis setup first. After data showed it met 95% of needs, we dropped the custom work and fixed the auth path instead.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you kept the customer and the product in mind when others wanted to chase a technically interesting problem. How did you steer the conversation?
Role: new engineer on small service team
Situation: teammates pushed custom cache for novelty
Action: surfaced real support data and proposed benchmark
Outcome: team shipped auth fix, no new layer
Quote: 'Support tickets showed login issues, not scale.'
Follow-up: Asked how they handled pushback; candidate said they asked for data review and deferred to metrics.
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Rocket engineering, not rocket science for the question about steering away from technically interesting problems. The candidate described pulling support tickets on login latency instead of letting the team build a custom cache. They ran a quick benchmark on existing Redis and convinced the group to fix auth instead. This shows early ownership of customer signals over personal technical curiosity. The story stays within individual scope but demonstrates coachability by using data to align the team. Biggest strength is grounding the decision in tickets rather than opinion.

lowerTranscript.text: The team wanted to try a new graph database for a feature. I mentioned customers might not care but went along since it was interesting.
I didn't push hard. We built a prototype and later realized it added complexity without customer benefit.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you kept the customer and the product in mind when others wanted to chase a technically interesting problem. How did you steer the conversation?
Role: new engineer
Situation: graph DB idea floated for unclear need
Action: voiced mild concern then participated
Outcome: prototype built, later scrapped for complexity
Quote: 'I mentioned customers might not care but went along.'
Follow-up: Asked what they would do differently; candidate said they would speak up more but had no concrete example.
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Rocket engineering, not rocket science for the question about steering away from technically interesting problems. The candidate noted a possible mismatch with customers yet still joined the graph database prototype effort. The work was later discarded after complexity surfaced. No evidence of using customer data or metrics to redirect the discussion. The response shows passive participation rather than ownership of the product direction. Biggest gap is lack of any steering action or follow-through on the initial concern.

raiseTranscript.text: Two teams wanted to adopt a new streaming framework for a shared pipeline because it had advanced features. I pulled usage data showing 80% of calls came from three simple endpoints.
How did you influence the outcome?
I ran a cross-team review with the data and proposed extending the current REST layer. We avoided the migration and used the saved cycles to improve error handling that customers actually hit.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you kept the customer and the product in mind when others wanted to chase a technically interesting problem. How did you steer the conversation?
Role: senior engineer across two teams
Situation: streaming framework proposed for novelty
Action: surfaced usage data and ran cross-team review
Outcome: extended REST instead, improved error handling
Quote: '80% of calls came from three simple endpoints.'
Follow-up: Asked about metrics; candidate shared before/after support ticket reduction on errors.
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Rocket engineering, not rocket science for the question about steering away from technically interesting problems. The candidate used endpoint usage data to show that a new streaming framework was unnecessary for most traffic. They led a cross-team review that resulted in extending the existing REST layer and redirecting effort to error handling. This produced measurable reduction in support tickets. The example demonstrates influence without authority and cross-team impact. Biggest strength is tying the decision directly to usage patterns and downstream customer benefit.

lowerTranscript.text: Engineering wanted to move to event sourcing for better auditability. I agreed it was technically clean but noted customers rarely asked for history.
We discussed it in a couple meetings. The team decided to prototype anyway and the work stayed in the backlog.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you kept the customer and the product in mind when others wanted to chase a technically interesting problem. How did you steer the conversation?
Role: senior engineer
Situation: event sourcing idea raised for audit features
Action: raised customer concern in meetings
Outcome: prototype approved, work lingered in backlog
Quote: 'Customers rarely asked for history.'
Follow-up: Asked for any follow-up data or decision; candidate had none beyond the initial discussion.
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Rocket engineering, not rocket science for the question about steering away from technically interesting problems. The candidate flagged that customers did not request audit history yet allowed the event sourcing prototype to proceed after a few meetings. No usage data or customer impact metrics were introduced to change the direction. The outcome left technical work in the backlog without resolution. The story shows awareness of the mismatch but no effective influence or cross-team leverage. Biggest gap is absence of concrete steering actions or results.

raiseTranscript.text: Leadership pushed for a new ML inference platform to explore advanced models. I reviewed the three-year roadmap and saw our core growth came from two existing product lines with stable predictions.

I redirected the investment to hardening the current inference service and added a small experiments budget instead. This kept reliability high for paying customers while still allowing limited exploration.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you kept the customer and the product in mind when others wanted to chase a technically interesting problem. How did you steer the conversation?
Role: director-level
Situation: ML platform proposed at org level
Action: reviewed roadmap, limited new spend to experiments budget
Outcome: hardened existing service, protected core revenue
Quote: 'Core growth came from two existing product lines.'
Follow-up: Asked about business impact; candidate cited retained ARR from improved uptime.
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Rocket engineering, not rocket science for the question about steering away from technically interesting problems. The candidate reviewed the three-year roadmap and determined that a new ML inference platform would not serve the two product lines driving growth. They limited the effort to a small experiments budget and redirected resources to hardening the existing service. This protected reliability for the main revenue base. The decision reflects strategic judgment and long-term trade-offs at org scale. Biggest strength is using roadmap data to set boundaries rather than allowing open-ended technical exploration.

lowerTranscript.text: The org wanted to build a custom orchestration layer for future flexibility. I asked about customer demand but the momentum was strong so we funded a pilot.
How did it affect the business?
The pilot ran for nine months. We later scaled it back after realizing it did not move any key product metrics.
